body.hook: Every drop of rain that falls on your school eventually flows somewhere: down a storm drain, into a creek, a river and finally an ocean. The land that drains into one river is its watershed, and we all live in one.

Water that flows over land instead of soaking in.

study.title: Where Does Our Water Go?
study.question: What is our watershed, and how does it connect us?
study.passage:
Watershed guide (written for this lesson from public sources):
Alberta's major river basins include the Peace, Athabasca, Hay, North Saskatchewan, South Saskatchewan (including the Bow, Oldman and Red Deer rivers), Beaver and Milk river basins.
Three oceans: water from the Peace and Athabasca flows north through the Mackenzie system to the Arctic Ocean; the Saskatchewan rivers flow east to Hudson Bay; the Milk River flows south to the Missouri and Mississippi and on to the Gulf of Mexico.
Headwaters: many of Alberta's rivers begin in the Rocky Mountains, fed by snowpack and glaciers.
Activities: 1. Crumpled-paper model: crumple paper, flatten partly, mark ridges with a blue marker, spray with water and watch where it flows and pools. Identify divides, tributaries and the "main river." 2. On a map of Alberta, find your river basin and trace your river to the ocean. 3. Local map: mark your school, the nearest creek or river, storm drains around the school and where they lead. 4. Discuss: what we put on driveways and lawns can end up in the river.
study.source: Summary written for this lesson from public Alberta government watershed information.
steps: Find your river basin on a map
Trace your river to the ocean

body.objective: Students will be able to test water quality.
successCriteria: I can test water for temperature, pH, turbidity and dissolved oxygen

body.hook: Water can look clear and still be unhealthy. Scientists test temperature, oxygen, pH and the tiny creatures living on the stream bottom to find out how healthy a waterway really is.

vocabulary.definition: How healthy water is for living things and people.
A scale from 0 to 14 showing how acidic or basic water is; 7 is neutral.
Oxygen mixed in water that fish and insects breathe.
Organisms whose presence shows environmental conditions.
Small animals without backbones living on stream bottoms, such as insect larvae.

study.title: Testing the Water
study.question: How healthy is our local water?
study.passage:
Water testing (written for this lesson; done with adult supervision at a safe, shallow site or with samples collected by staff):
Tests: 1. Temperature (thermometer): cold water holds more oxygen; trout prefer cold water. 2. pH (test strips): many healthy streams range from about 6.5 to 8.5. 3. Turbidity (turbidity tube or a Secchi disk): cloudier water can mean erosion or runoff. 4. Dissolved oxygen (test kit): most fish need more than about 5 mg/L; cold-water fish need more.
Invertebrates: gently kick-net a riffle, put the catch in a white tray with water, identify with a key, and return everything. Sensitive to pollution: mayfly, stonefly and caddisfly larvae. Somewhat tolerant: dragonfly larvae, scuds, crayfish. Tolerant: aquatic worms, leeches, midge larvae. Many sensitive species = good water quality.
Safety: no wading in fast or deep water; wash hands; wear boots.
Analysis: compare results with healthy ranges; suggest causes (e.g. low oxygen in warm, slow water; high turbidity after rain).
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; ranges are general guides used in stream monitoring education.
steps: Test temperature, pH, turbidity and oxygen
discussion: Which test result was outside the healthy range?
What invertebrates did you find, and what do they indicate?
What could improve water quality here?
study.product: Write a water-quality report with test results, invertebrate findings, an overall health rating and two suggested causes or actions.

body.objective: Students will be able to track local wildlife.
successCriteria: I can identify common Alberta animal tracks and signs
I can record wildlife observations in a survey
I can explain how wildlife depends on habitat and connected corridors
body.hook: Most wild animals avoid people, but they leave clues everywhere: tracks in mud and snow, chewed twigs, scat, feathers and trails. Learning to read these signs lets you discover who shares your neighbourhood.

vocabulary.definition: A footprint left by an animal.
Any evidence of an animal, such as scat, chewing, nests or trails.
The place an animal lives and finds food, water, shelter and space.
A connected strip of habitat that lets animals move safely.
Seasonal movement of animals from one area to another.
Projects where the public collects data for scientists.

study.title: Who Lives Here?
study.question: How can I find and record local wildlife?
study.passage:
Tracking guide (written for this lesson):
Common Alberta tracks: deer: split heart shape (two toes). Coyote: oval with four toes and claw marks, often in a straight line. Domestic dog: rounder, toes more spread, wandering path. Snowshoe hare: large hind feet landing in front of small front feet (a Y-shaped pattern). Squirrel: small, with front and hind feet in a box pattern. Birds: three forward toes, one back.
Other signs: chewed cones (squirrels), browsed twigs (deer, hares), woodpecker holes, scat, feathers, nests, trails through grass.
Survey (40 minutes): along a set route near school or a park, record each sign: type, location, size (photo with a ruler or a coin for scale), likely animal and confidence (sure, probably, unsure). Never touch scat.
Habitat needs: food, water, shelter, space. Roads and buildings can break habitat into pieces; wildlife corridors and crossings (like those on the Trans-Canada Highway in Banff National Park) help animals move.
Citizen science: share observations with projects like iNaturalist (with a teacher account) so scientists can use the data.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; tracking descriptions are general field-guide features.
steps: Survey a route and record signs
discussion: Which animal signs were most common?
How sure were you of each identification?
What habitat features supported these animals?
How could a wildlife corridor help animals near our school?
study.product: Complete a wildlife sign survey with at least six records, then explain what habitat features support the animals you found.
